## Problem 1 - Birthday Paradox Findings
The birthday paradox is the notion that for a randomly selected group of individuals, there is ~51% chance that at least two people in the group share the same birthday. Lets find out more about this!

```{r, echo = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
# Make a function for the birthday paradox itself
birthday_pardox = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  length(birthdays) > length(unique(birthdays))
}


# Run the function 10,000 times (group size: 2-50)
paradox_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    n = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) %>% 
  mutate(result 
         = map_lgl(n, birthday_pardox)) %>% 
  group_by(n) %>% 
  summarize(prob = mean(result))
```


```{r}
# Plot the birthday paradox!
paradox_results_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = prob)) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63919", linewidth = 1.5) + 
  geom_point(color = "#ffb711", size = 1.7) +       
  labs(
    title = "The Birthday Paradox",
    subtitle = "Based on 10,000 Simulations for Groups of 2-50",
    x = "Group Size (N)",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1d3551"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#457b9a")
  )
```


#### Figure 1 - Interpretation
Guided by the Birthday Paradox, this figure highlights that as the size of a group increases, the probability of at least two individuals sharing a birthday increases (not linear manner). This aligns with our understanding because the number of possible pairs of individuals grows quickly rather than linearly with group size.



## Problem 2 - RCT Longitudinal Data
```{r, echo = FALSE}
# Create a df with all RCT data
path_to_data = "./data/" 
all_files = list.files(path = path_to_data, full.names = FALSE)

file_df = tibble(file_name = all_files)


# Read in using purrr::map
parsed_data = 
  file_df %>% 
  mutate(
    file_path = 
      str_c(path_to_data, file_name),
    data = map(file_path, ~read_csv(.x, show_col_types = FALSE))
  ) %>% 
  unnest(data)


# Tidy this df to prepare for data viz
tidy_df = parsed_data %>% 
  mutate(
    file_name = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$"),
    arm = str_sub(file_name, 1, 3),
    arm = if_else(arm == "con", "Control", "Experimental"),
    subject_id = str_sub(file_name, 5, 8)
  ) %>% 
  select(arm, subject_id, everything(), -file_path, -file_name) %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) %>% 
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week))
```



```{r}
# Plot the results 
tidy_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes
         (x = week, y = observation, group = interaction(arm, subject_id), color = arm)) +
  geom_path(alpha = 1, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~arm) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#ffb711", "Experimental" = "#e63919")) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Randomized Control Trial",
    subtitle = "Comparing the Control and Experimental Study Arms",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Value",
    color = "Arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1d3551"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#457b9a"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

#### Figure 2 - Interpretation
Based on this spaghetti plot, participants in the control arm of the RCT maintained relatively stable/similar over time. In contrast, participants in the experimental arm exhibited a general upward trend in values over time, with the divergence becoming especially pronounced around the 2- to 4-week mark of the study.



## Problem 3 - T-Test
```{r, echo = FALSE}
# Function for a one-sample t-test
sim_t_test = function
(n = 30, mu, sigma = 5) {
  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )
  
  t_test_results = t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0) %>% 
    broom::tidy()
  
  tibble(
    mu_hat = t_test_results$estimate,
    p_value = t_test_results$p.value
  )
}


# Run the simulation
set.seed(1)

sim_power_df = 
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    result = map(true_mu, ~sim_t_test(n = 30, mu = .x, sigma = 5))
  ) %>% 
  unnest(result)
```


### Problem 3.1 - Power vs. Effect Size Figure
```{r}
power_df = sim_power_df %>% 
  group_by(true_mu) %>% 
  summarize(power = mean(p_value < 0.05))

power_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63919", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(color = "#ffb711", size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Power of One-Sample T-Test",
    subtitle = 
      "Null hypothesis (H0: μ = 0) was rejected (α=0.05, n=30, σ=5)",
    x = "True Value of μ (Effect Size)",
    y = "Power"
  ) +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1d3551"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#457b9a")
  )
```

#### Figure 3.1 - Interpretation
As the true value of μ increases, the power of the test also increases, reflecting a higher probability of rejecting the false null hypothesis. The power curve increases as the effect size increases, eventually leveling off ~1.0 (100% power) once the true value reaches approximately 4.



### Problem 3.2 - Average Estimate of μ Hat Figure
```{r}
# Prepare df for data viz
estimate_df = sim_power_df %>% 
  group_by(true_mu) %>% 
  summarize(
    avg_mu_hat_all = mean(mu_hat),
    avg_mu_hat_rejected = mean(mu_hat[p_value < 0.05])
  ) %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("avg_mu_hat"),
    names_to = "subset",
    values_to = "mean_estimate"
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    subset = if_else(subset == "avg_mu_hat_all", "All Samples", "Samples with Rejected Null")
  )

# Plot results
estimate_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = mean_estimate, color = subset)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "#afd711") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("All Samples" = "#ffb711", "Samples with Rejected Null" = "#e63919")) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimate of μ̂ vs. True μ",
    subtitle = "Comparing subsets where the null was rejected",
    x = "True Value of μ",
    y = "Average Estimate of μ̂",
    color = "Subset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1d3551"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#457b9a"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

#### Figure 3.2 - Interpretation
Across the samples, the average estimate of μ hat generally follows the true value of μ. This shows that the sample mean estimator is unbiased. However, when restricting the analysis to samples where the null hypothesis was rejected, the average estimate of μ hat is overestimated relative to the true value when the effect size is small. As the true value increases, power approaches 1.0, causing the lines to converge.


## Problem 3.3 - Write Up
**Question 1:** 
As the true value of μ increases (larger effect size), the power of the one-sample t-test increases. When the true effect size equals 0 (null hypothesis is true), the rejection rate is at the typical significance level in public health literature (α=0.05). The t-test becomes better at rejecting the false null hypothesis, eventually ~100% power at μ≥4.

**Question 2:**
Across samples, the average estimate of μ hat is ~ equal to the true value of 
μ, confirming that the sample mean is an unbiased estimator. 
For the subset of samples where the null hypothesis is rejected, the average estimate of μ hat is overestimated when the true effect size is small.This discrepancy is often due to selection bias. When power is low, a t-test only achieves statistical significance by chance if random sampling error. As the true effect size increases and power approaches ~1.0, nearly all samples are able to reject the null, eliminating this conditional bias and causing the lines to converge on the plots.
